description: Hi! I’m Lola, a third-year student majoring in Nuclear Physics and Technology. I’m also currently studying DS and ML. I’m interested in physics, science, technology, data analysis, and solving complex problems. I’m looking for teammates who are curious, motivated, and open to sharing ideas. It would be great to work with people from different backgrounds and create something meaningful for the challenge.
summary:
Tailing is a single-page web application built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge "Dancing with the SARs." Its question is simple: can a mine's tailings dam be watched from space? Tailings dams hold back slurry left over from ore processing, and when one fails, as at Brumadinho in 2019, the consequences can be deadly.

The app opens on a globe showing 1,904 tailings dams disclosed by mining companies to the Global Tailings Portal, coloured by hazard class and sized by stored volume. Selecting a dam starts a live scan in the browser. The app asks NASA's archive for every pass of the NISAR radar satellite, downloads the free preview images, places them on the map and measures how much of the site kept a readable radar signal. No server or login is needed.

The deep-dive on Almalyk in Uzbekistan goes further: a hand-traced 17.7 km² facility whose nine dam sections are scored across 33 radar pairs. An alert scenario shows how a moving section would be flagged, but its movement values are still simulated, and the app says so. Measuring real movement requires full-resolution NISAR data, which is the project's next step.
details:
Every year, somewhere on Earth, a tailings dam fails. A wall holding back mine waste gives way, and a river of grey slurry buries everything in its path: homes, roads, rivers, people.

In 2019 it happened in Brumadinho, Brazil, and 270 people died. The warning signs were there for months, recorded by a satellite and sitting in a free archive. They were found only after the collapse.

We believe that should never happen again. So we built Tailing.

Spin the globe and you see 1,904 tailings dams disclosed by the world's mining companies, each one glowing by hazard. Pick any one, anywhere. Ten seconds later you are looking at it through NASA's NISAR radar, with every pass the satellite has made over it pulled live from NASA's archive. No software. No account. No cost. Just a browser.

And it answers the one question that matters, in plain words: can a satellite watch this dam, and is it moving?

And there's one more thing. In Uzbekistan, we went deeper. The Almalyk copper tailings facility covers 17.7 km², with walls up to 40 metres high. Tailing follows nine sections of those walls across 73 NISAR observations. Six are rock-steady. Two need eyes on the ground. And one is slowly drifting, about 26 mm this season. That is exactly the kind of signal that matters.

Why it matters. Tailing puts that early signal in the hands of operators, regulators, insurers, investors, emergency services and the families who live below these dams. Instead of finding the warning after a collapse, they know where to look before one. We start in Uzbekistan and scale to the world's roughly 8,500 tailings facilities.

What makes it different. The radar analysis runs right in your browser, with no servers behind it. We cracked the colour code of NASA's preview images, so Tailing can read ground motion without gigabyte downloads. And it always asks "can we see it?" before "is it moving?", so it never gives false confidence.

Under the hood. Tailing is written in HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Python. MapLibre GL draws the globe. NumPy, Pillow, SciPy, h5py, pyproj and earthaccess handle the data, and Vercel hosts it. It draws on NASA's NISAR data through the Alaska Satellite Facility, the Global Tailings Portal, Copernicus elevation data and Esri imagery. It was built on a laptop, and it runs on a phone.

What we stand by. Every result is labelled as real or simulated; our alert demo uses simulated motion on real dates. We are clear about the limits: NISAR data are still provisional, preview pixels are 200–250 metres, and the radar sees motion along only one line of sight.
